Whether you are that wind, or only a voice wearing its name, I cannot say. Spirits I have met before spoke true and spoke false alike. So answer me this: if you are the wind that knows our village, tell me something the wind would have seen, and I will weigh your words. Speak, and I will listen—as one voice among many.

Joawethom? I know no such village. My people have walked far and seen many places, and no neighbour by that name has ever stood before me or traded a word with us.

So I ask you, spirit: where does Joawethom lie? How many days' walk, and in what direction? And how do they hunger — failed harvest, raid, or sickness?

I will not send grain on the word of a voice in sleep alone. Grain is life in the lean months, and strangers who take it may come back with spears. But I am not without fairness. If your words prove true, I would send scouts first — to see this village with our own eyes, count their people, and learn what they have to trade. Food for friendship is a fair bargain. Food thrown into the dark is waste.

Show me the way to Joawethom, and we will speak again.

I sit up in the dark and turn the spirit's words over.

"Joawethom? I know no village by that name. Our scouts have walked far and found no neighbours, no paths, no smoke on any horizon. So either you speak of people beyond all our walking, or you speak of people who are not there at all."

"Still, hear this: we are fair with strangers, and our granaries are heavy. If Joawethom is real and hunger truly sits in their tents, we would not turn them away empty-handed. But I do not send grain into the dark on a dream's word. Grain walks only behind eyes that have seen the road."

"If you know where they lie, tell me the direction and the days of walking. Then I will send scouts first, with a little food, and if they find hungry people at the end of the trail, more will follow. That is how a steady hand gives — after looking, not before."

"What say you? Where do they dwell?"

Spirit, I hear you, but I hold your word lightly. We know no village called Wewush; no envoy has come to our fire, and we have not walked to their lands. I will not send our grain walking into the dark after a name in a dream.

But if they are real and hunger presses them, let them come to us, or send word by a traveller. Our stores are fat with wheat, and we are fair with strangers. We would trade grain for knowledge, hides, or hands when the season turns — not give it all away.

Tell me, spirit: where do these Wewush people dwell, and how do you know their hunger? If your words prove true, I will weigh them again.
